cards.explanation: The feast is the Passover, friends. The king commands all the people, “Keep the Passover of the LORD your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant.” Josiah isn't making up a party. He's pointing at the page and saying, "It's right HERE." Even a stamper who spent years in a junk drawer knows you follow the recipe.

The answer is the days of the judges, friends. The text says no such Passover had been observed “…from the days of the judges who had governed Israel through all the days of the kings of Israel and Judah.” Think about how long that stretch is. It starts with the judges and runs through the kings of Israel and Judah, and this Passover in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign is the one the text sets apart.

The answer is False, friends. The text says this Passover was observed to the LORD in Jerusalem, not at Bethel. Bethel is where Josiah was busy tearing down an altar (2 Kings 23:15). Wrecking crew in one town, feast in another.

The answer is mediums and household idols, bakers. The text says Josiah removed the mediums and spiritists, the household gods and idols, and “…all the abominations that were seen in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem.” Notice it says all the abominations, not just a few. I think Josiah wasn't skipping anything.

The missing word is law, friends. Josiah did all of this to carry out “…the words of the law written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had found in the house of the LORD.” He didn't stop at hearing it. He carried it out. That's what all the clearing out was for.

The answer is True, friends. The text says, “Neither before nor after Josiah was there any king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength, according to all the Law of Moses.” Before AND after, and that's a whole lot of kings. The writer doesn't hand out that kind of line easily.

The missing word is Moses, bakers. Josiah turned to the LORD with all his heart, soul and strength, “…according to all the Law of Moses.” All his heart, all his soul, all his strength, and the whole Law. I can barely finish a whole batch without a snack break.

The answer is False, friends. The text says, “Nevertheless, the LORD did not turn away from the fury of His burning anger, which was kindled against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done to provoke Him to anger.” It's a heavy turn after all that good news about Josiah. I think this one is a lot to take in.

The name is Manasseh, bakers. The text says the anger was “…kindled against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done to provoke Him to anger.” Manasseh was a king of Judah before Josiah (2 Kings 21:1). The writer doesn't hide whose doing this was.

The answer is that He would remove Judah from His sight as He did Israel, bakers. The LORD had said, “I will remove Judah from My sight, just as I removed Israel.” That's heavy, and I think it hurts to read. It's what He had already said.

The answer is True, friends. The LORD had said, “I will reject this city Jerusalem, which I chose, and the temple of which I said, ‘My Name shall be there.’…” That includes the city He chose and the temple where He said His Name would be. It's a hard line to read, and I think it's meant to be.

The answer is the king of Assyria, bakers. The text says Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt marched up to help the king of Assyria at the Euphrates River. The king of Assyria is the one Neco is going to help. Josiah then goes out to confront Neco, and that's the next turn in the story.

The missing word is Jerusalem, friends. The text says that from Megiddo his servants carried his body in a chariot, brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own tomb. His servants carry him all the way home. I think that's a sad, quiet trip.

The answer is a son of Josiah, bakers. The text calls him “…Jehoahaz son of Josiah…” The people of the land took him, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father. So a son takes his father's place.
